findings.title: The cause suffix logic is written twice, once in the Ukrainian cellLabel and once in the English table
findings.evidence: `const suffix = given ? `, ${CELL.given}` : (hinted ? `, ${CELL.hint}` : '') + (cause ? `, ${CELL.cause}` : '');` appears again almost word for word at line 163 with `EN_CELL`. The duplication existed before this change, but this change adds a third flag and a precedence rule (a given wins; the hint comes before the cause) to both copies. The rule now lives in two places that have to stay in step. The parity tests catch drift only for the sample calls they make.
findings.suggestion: Write one helper, e.g. `buildCellLabel(table, row, col, value, given, hinted, cause)`, and call it from both `cellLabel` and `EN.cellLabel`, passing the `CELL` or `EN_CELL` table.
verifierNotes: The duplication is real. Line 32 builds the suffix from CELL and line 163 builds it from EN_CELL with identical logic. Both copies now carry the added cause flag and the same precedence: a given cell wins, then the hint, then the cause. The two copies agree today and the ternary binds as intended, so no behavioural defect exists. This is a maintainability and drift-risk finding, not a correctness bug. It is labelled as correctness but is really a minor cleanup, and it was already duplicated before this change.

Confirmed by reading src/ui/strings.ts. Line 32 (Ukrainian cellLabel, using CELL) and line 163 (EN.cellLabel, using EN_CELL) contain the same suffix expression and the same return template. The only difference is the table they read from. The precedence rule is the same in both copies: a given cell wins, and otherwise the hint comes before the cause. A change to that rule has to be made twice. This is a maintainability risk, not a user-visible bug. Both copies are currently correct and agree with each other, so no real user hits a wrong label today. The finding is valid as a minor duplication issue.

findings.title: The theme-and-size stills show the cause cell with the hover ring on, so the triangle is never seen on its own
findings.evidence: Smoke-test step 10 lists stills/smoke-{6x6,8x8}-{light,dark}-{375,1024,320}.png and the two 4x4 stills as the plain theme-and-size evidence, separate from the *-hover-x3 stills. In every one of them, the cause cell (the third 0 of the run, or (3,1) at 4x4) has an inner tan/brown ring that its violating neighbours lack. A 3x zoom of smoke-6x6-light-1024.png shows it clearly, and it shows at 8x8 dark 320 too. This is the --color-hover-ring inset: the Playwright click leaves the pointer over the cell, and smoke-sweep.mjs moves the mouse only for the dedicated 1024 hover shot. At 8x8 on 320 (an 8px leg, in the same #ff8a7d as the cell's own border), the hover ring is the more visible thing that sets the cause cell apart in these frames. So the stills overstate how findable the mark is for a touch user, who gets no hover ring. The step-10 claim, 'small but findable: a red corner on the third cell of the run', rests on frames where the ring also marks that cell.
findings.suggestion: Re-capture the theme/size stills with the pointer moved off the board (for example page.mouse.move(0,0) and a short wait) before each screenshot, and above all 8x8 light/dark at 320. findings.title: The checker runs twice per press: breaksRule repeats the findViolations call that refreshHighlights just made
findings.evidence: `breaksRule` does `return findViolations(board).some(...)`, and both the click handler and the hint handler call it right after `refreshHighlights()`, which has already run `for (const v of findViolations(board))` on the same board. The result is correct, because the cause cells (`v.cells`) are always a subset of the highlighted set (the count rule highlights the whole line). Still, every press runs the full checker twice, and the two places that read violations can drift apart if one of them changes.

findings.title: The e2e reads the ::after content but never asserts it
findings.evidence: `return { borderTopWidth: s.borderTopWidth, content: s.content };` reads `content`, but only `pseudo.borderTopWidth` is used, in the annotation and in the soft assertion at line 264. If `content` were dropped from the rule (e.g. it became `none`), the pixel read would catch it, but the value that is read here goes unchecked, so it is dead data.
findings.suggestion: Either remove `content` from the evaluate result, or add a soft assertion that it equals `'""'`, as a second check alongside the pixel (the secondary role the spec allows).
verifierNotes: The finding's central claim is false. It says only `pseudo.borderTopWidth` is used, but line 254 interpolates `pseudo.content` into the `pixels` annotation (`(content ${pseudo.content})`). So `content` is not dead data. It is recorded as diagnostic evidence next to the width. The test's primary assertion is the corner pixel colour (lines 257-259), and the spec text says the computed-style check is the secondary one. If `content` became `none`, the `::after` would not render and the pixel assertion would fail. A missing soft assertion on `content` is therefore redundant and not a correctness defect in the e2e. At most it is a stylistic nit, and the evidence given is wrong.

The code at e2e/nfr-14-cause-mark.spec.ts:249 does read `content` and never asserts it. But the finding's claim that it is "dead data" is wrong. The value is interpolated into the `pixels` annotation (`::after border-top-width ... (content ${pseudo.content})`), so it is recorded as diagnostic evidence in the test report. The finding itself concedes that the corner-pixel assertion would catch a dropped or `none` content, because the mark would not render. The primary assertion therefore already covers the failure it worries about, and the comment says the borderTopWidth check is only a secondary assertion. No user-visible or test-escape failure follows from reading `content` without asserting it. It is at most a style nit about adding a redundant assertion, not a defect that can occur.
